summary: The rule '%s packs every path its manifest promises' re-implements the `files` glob in `packedBy()` and asks it whether npm WOULD pack the path — it never consults `PACKED`, the real `npm pack --dry-run` listing the same file already computes at line 207. Its sibling rule checks only that a SOURCE exists (`builtFrom` maps `./dist/index.js` -> `src/index.ts`). So a build that emits a different layout than `exports` promises, or that emits nothing, passes. Compounding it: nothing anywhere in the repo ever imports the built `dist/index.js` (grep for `await import(.*dist)` across all `*.test.ts` returns nothing) — every test imports `src/`, so the published entrypoint is never executed. That is also why `version.ts`'s whole reason for existing is ungraded: `src/../package.json` resolves correctly no matter what `dist/` looks like, and mutating `CORE_VERSION` to a fixed wrong string leaves the entire bridge-core suite green.
failure: Reproduced: `mv packages/bridge-core/dist/index.js` and `dist/index.d.ts` out of the tree, then run packaging.test.ts — 72/72 tests pass. `@sharptrick/parley-core` would publish with `exports['.'] = {types: './dist/index.d.ts', default: './dist/index.js'}` pointing at two files that are not in the tarball; every consumer's `import ... from '@sharptrick/parley-core'` fails with ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND. `filesUnder()` also returns `[]` when `dist` is absent entirely, so the artifact rule is green on an unbuilt tree too.

Add one row per public workspace that actually loads the artifact: `await import(pathToFileURL(join(REPO_ROOT, w.dir, exportsDefault)))` and asserts it resolves and, for core, that `CORE_VERSION === manifest.version`.

The doc is what routed them there.

summary: startPresenceLoop guards heartbeatMs only at the LOW end (`< 1`, non-finite). Node's setInterval truncates any delay above 2147483647 to 1 ms, so a config-legal `presence.heartbeat_ms` above 2^31-1 produces exactly the post storm the guard's own comment says it prevents. `presence.heartbeat_ms` in config.ts is `z.number().int().positive()` with no `.max()`, unlike its sibling `catchup.block_max_ms` which is `.max(MAX_BLOCK_MS)`. The same shape applies to `goodbyeTimeoutMs` fed to setTimeout in `bounded()`.
failure: config `presence: { heartbeat_ms: 2147483648 }` (or any value > 2147483647; ~24.8 days) -> reproduced against startPresenceLoop with a FakePlugin: 268 `plugin.post` calls to the shared presence topic in 300 ms (~890/s), plus a TimeoutOverflowWarning on stderr. Every peer's `parley_list_users` reads that topic, so one mis-set instance floods the roster page for the whole deployment and its own `truncated` flag hides quieter peers.
remediation: Add the upper bound where the lower one lives: `if (!Number.isFinite(opts.heartbeatMs) || opts.heartbeatMs < 1 || opts.heartbeatMs > 2_147_483_647) throw new RangeError(...)`, and mirror it in config.ts as `heartbeat_ms: z.number().int().positive().max(2_147_483_647, { message: ... })` so an operator fails at load rather than at attach. Do the same for `PresenceLoopOptions.goodbyeTimeoutMs` (it reaches setTimeout in `bounded()` with the identical truncation).
testUpgrade: degenerate-bounds.test.ts already tables every embedder-facing sizing knob against values that DELETE the feature; it only tables the low end. Give `Knob` a `degenerate` list that is generated per knob from a shared vector — `[0, -1, 0.5, NaN, ±Infinity, 2**31, 2**31 + 1, Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER]` — for every knob whose value reaches a Node timer, and add a `timerBacked: true` marker so the table asserts the 2^31 rows too. That widened generator also covers `goodbyeTimeoutMs`, `block_poll_interval_ms` and any future cadence knob without a new case.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: Nothing new. It extends the existing `if (!Number.isFinite(opts.heartbeatMs) || opts.heartbeatMs < 1)` branch in startPresenceLoop, and (for the config half) the same `.max(...)` pattern config.ts already uses for `block_max_ms`.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: `startPresenceLoop(..., { heartbeatMs: 2_147_483_648 })` and `presence.heartbeat_ms` above 2147483647 in a config file — today both are accepted and become a 1 ms beat loop.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found. I applied the presence-loop half verbatim and ran the whole bridge-core suite: 56 files / 3386 tests passed. degenerate-bounds.test.ts's `legal: 600_000` control and presence-loop.test.ts's small cadences are all far below the new ceiling. I did not apply the config.ts `.max()` half, so config.test.ts is untested against it.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If applied and the storm still happened it would mean the truncation came from somewhere other than setInterval; nothing else in the module is bounded by this check, so there is no symptom left hidden.

summary: `fetchRecentBlocking` returns the moment `result.messages.length > 0`, without applying the topic filter that every other core path applies to a plugin page. On a backend whose history read is coarser than a topic — the shape core ships a fake for (`coarseDelivery` in testing/nonconformant.ts) and which tools.ts, push-loop.ts and list-users-tool.ts each call "the same trust boundary" — a page of purely foreign-topic traffic reads as "a message arrived". tools.ts then filters it all out, so the caller gets an empty page and the long poll silently collapsed into a single fetch.
failure: A Matrix-room / NATS-wildcard-shaped plugin whose page for topic `ctx` carries only messages on `other-room-topic`. `parley_fetch_recent({ topic: 'ctx', block_ms: 3000 })` -> reproduced end-to-end through the MCP client: returned after 1 ms with `{ messages: [] }` and exactly 1 plugin `fetchRecent` call, instead of holding ~3000 ms. Every foreign message on the shared room restarts the agent's poll, which is precisely the "a polling agent burns tokens per message, not per tick" behaviour TOOL_TEXT.fetch_recent promises block_ms prevents.
remediation: Decide arrival on the topic that was asked for: `if (result.messages.some((m) => m.topic === args.topic)) return result;` at blocking-fetch.ts:128. `since = result.nextCursor` already advances past the discarded foreign rows, so nothing is re-scanned and no cursor is invented. Leave the drop-count log in tools.ts where it is; it still fires on the returned page.
testUpgrade: coarse-delivery.test.ts already tables the trust boundary over PATHS × foreign-topic kinds and states that "a guard added to one sibling and not the other is exactly the defect". Its PATHS list is missing a cell. Add `parley_fetch_recent WITH block_ms` as a third path, and make the coarse fake parameterizable over whether the page carries the requested topic at all (`coarseDelivery({ carryOwn: false })`), so the table asserts both "only the asked-for topic reaches the agent" and "a page with none of it does not end a long poll early". That widened fake also lets the existing non-blocking rows exercise an all-foreign page, which none of them do today.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `FetchRecentArgs.topic` (already in scope as `args.topic`; the loop only overrides `since`/`blockMs`) and the existing `since = result.nextCursor` advance on line 131, which is what keeps the discarded foreign rows from being re-read.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: A page containing only foreign-topic messages no longer terminates the poll. A direct embedder of the exported `fetchRecentBlocking` that deliberately drives a coarse plugin and reads the raw page would now wait out its budget instead of getting that page back immediately.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found. I applied this exact edit and ran the whole bridge-core suite: 56 files / 3386 tests passed. I specifically checked blocking-fetch.test.ts, tools.test.ts, absent-topic-sites.test.ts, tool-outcomes.test.ts and root-teardown-bounds.test.ts (the five files that touch blockMs) and grepped for any assertion on the "dropped N fetched message(s)" log — there is none. summary: terminalErrorHandler logs the whole error object. body-parser attaches the RAW request body to `entity.parse.failed`/`parameters.too.many` errors (node_modules/body-parser/lib/read.js: `next(createError(400, err, { body: str, type: ... }))`), and Node's console.error prints an Error's own enumerable properties. On the built-in OAuth front door those bodies are exactly the credential-bearing ones — `/parley/consent` carries `passphrase`, `/token` carries `refresh_token`/`code_verifier`/`client_secret`. Worse, the SDK mounts `express.urlencoded` BEFORE its rate limiter (node_modules/@modelcontextprotocol/sdk/.../handlers/token.js), so a body-parser failure never reaches the limiter: an unauthenticated caller gets unbounded, unrate-limited, attacker-chosen log writes on a public endpoint.

summary: `endWithin`'s give-up path destroys `resource.connection.stream`, which only exists on a `pg.Client`. failure: Through a TCP proxy in front of a real server: connect({pool_size:1}) -> post() -> proxy.blackhole() -> a second post() parks with the pool's only client checked out -> disconnect(). remediation: Give `endWithin` a resource-kind-aware give-up: keep the current stream destroy for a `Client`, and for a `Pool` walk the clients it still owns and destroy each one's stream (pg-pool exposes them on the private `_clients` array), or pass an explicit `destroy` callback in from `open()`/`disconnect()` rather than sniffing shape. If neither is acceptable, correct connection.ts:77-83 and the README bullet to say the pooled path is bounded by `QUERY_WAIT_MS`, not by `TEARDOWN_WAIT_MS`.
testUpgrade: Parameterize the give-up path over RESOURCE KIND rather than over the call that was parked: a table of {pooled client with a statement in flight, pooled client idle, listener client with a query in flight, listener client idle} x {black-holed peer, silent peer}, each asserting after `await disconnect()` that no undestroyed socket to the fault's port remains in `process._getActiveHandles()` within a small grace. silent-peer.test.ts's `disconnect() returns without waiting for a parked %s` rows are too narrow: they assert only the ORDER in which disconnect and the parked call settle, which is satisfied whether or not the socket was destroyed.

summary: `retention_days` is destructive state shared by every session on the table, but the 'Multiple concurrent sessions' section lists only `url` and `table_name` as must-match and then explicitly blesses `pool_size` differing per session. summary: Every failure arm of `post()` tells the caller 'Nothing was written', including the arm where the lost answer belonged to `COMMIT` — a case in which the row may be durably committed. The same sentence is emitted by `fetchRecent`, where it is meaningless.
failure: post() runs BEGIN / lock_timeout / advisory lock / INSERT / COMMIT on one client. If the peer black-holes after the COMMIT reaches the server, `query_timeout` fires on the COMMIT, `answerNeverCame` is true, and the caller gets `parley-postgres: gave up on the write to topic 'x' after 15000ms — … Nothing was written; that connection has been discarded and a retry opens a new one.` The server has committed. An agent that believes the sentence retries and posts the message twice, under two different `backendMsgId`s, which core's dedup cannot collapse. The read path says the same thing: `parley-postgres: the fetch from topic 'x' failed — … Nothing was written` for a SELECT.
remediation: Track which statement is in flight in `post()` and, for a lost answer at or after COMMIT, say the write may or may not have landed and that the topic should be re-read before retrying. Drop the 'Nothing was written' clause from the read paths (`fetchRecent`, `resolveIdentity`'s SELECT) or make `serverRefused` take the clause as an argument.
testUpgrade: Parameterize on WHICH statement the answer is lost at — {before BEGIN, after BEGIN, after INSERT/before COMMIT, at COMMIT} x {black hole, admin kill} — using a proxy that starts dropping bytes after the Nth server response, and assert the rejection's durability claim matches what a follow-up `fetchRecent` from an independent connection actually finds. The current index-key-budget and silent-peer rows only assert the presence of the phrase (`toMatch(/[Nn]othing was written/)`), which is exactly the assertion that cements the wrong claim.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `answerAbandoned`/`answerNeverCame` in errors.ts (matching pg's 'Query read timeout') and the try/catch in post() at index.ts:294-308. Depends on the `answerNeverCame(err)` branch specifically — the lock-timeout and plain-refusal branches genuinely did write nothing and should keep their wording.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none — the same calls reject, with different text on one arm.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: index-key-budget.test.ts asserts `/[Nn]othing was written/` on post failures, but those cells fail at INSERT (index key refused) or at the first statement (relation gone), never at COMMIT, so they stay green. silent-peer.test.ts's rows assert only that the call settles. summary: The subscribe loop checks `isStale` immediately after the `/sync` response, then awaits `backfill()` (a full HTTP round-trip, and up to 50 pages), and then delivers with no second check. A `disconnect()` that lands inside that backfill is followed by the whole batch being handed to the caller's handler after `disconnect()` has already resolved. `backfill` compounds it by re-deriving `const generation = this.generation` instead of taking the loop's, so after a bare reconnect it happily pages under the NEW generation's credential while the loop it serves is stale.
failure: subscribe(topic) on a shared_room plugin, syncCap=1 so a 3-message burst arrives `limited`, the `dir=b&from=` backfill page held 800ms; call `disconnect()` while it is in flight. `disconnect()` resolves, and ~0ms later the handler fires three times with 'a','b','c'. Reproduced: the probe asserting `events.filter(e => e.at >= disconnectedAt)` is empty failed with all three messages present.
remediation: Add `if (this.isStale(generation)) break;` immediately before the `for (const e of [...recovered, ...events...])` delivery loop in `subscribe`, and pass the loop's `generation` into `backfill(roomId, topic, prevBatch, stopAfter, skip, generation)` instead of letting it read `this.generation` — so a stale loop's recovery neither runs under the next generation's token nor delivers what it recovered.
testUpgrade: CLASS: a delivery path that awaits anything between its staleness check and its handler call. `reconnect-lifecycle.fake.test.ts`'s `PARKED_IN` table has exactly two rows ('an in-flight /sync', 'the retry backoff') — neither has an await between the gate and the delivery, which is why it stays green. Widen that table into a generator over EVERY awaited point in the subscribe loop (positioning sync, incremental sync, the `limited` backfill, the inter-sync pace delay), each row landing the disconnect inside that await via `fake.holdMessages`/`stallPositioning` and asserting both `got === []` after the teardown AND that no request is issued past it. The same generator should be reused for `connect()`-without-`disconnect()`, which is the arm that catches the `backfill` generation re-derivation.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `MatrixSession.isStale`: `return this.stopped || this.generation !== generation;` — the `this.stopped` arm is what makes the plain-disconnect case break, the `generation !== generation` arm the reconnect case. Also relies on `backfill`'s existing loop guard `page < MAX_BACKFILL_PAGES && !this.isStale(generation)`, which with the threaded generation now refuses page 0 outright for a stale loop.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: A `limited`-burst batch whose backfill straddled a disconnect or reconnect is no longer delivered live. Those events stay reachable through `fetchRecent` catch-up — the same guarantee the pre-existing `catch { /* backfill is best-effort */ }` around backfill already leans on.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none — I applied both edits and ran the whole offline suite (`npx vitest run packages/bridge-matrix` minus the two live files): 20 files / 1104 tests passed, and my repro flipped from red to green.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Fixes it. If only the `break` were added and `backfill` kept `this.generation`, a stale loop's backfill would still issue up to 50 authenticated `/messages` pages under the next generation's token before the break stopped the delivery — work the teardown is supposed to have ended.
remediationCheck.interleavings: (1) disconnect lands while the backfill request is on the wire → request completes, loop's next guard is the new `break`, nothing delivered. (2) disconnect lands after backfill returns but before the `break` → same. (3) `connect()` with no disconnect lands mid-backfill → with the threaded generation, backfill's own loop guard trips at the top of its next page and it returns what it has; the `break` then discards it, while the NEW generation's loop (started by a fresh `subscribe`) is unaffected because it captured the new number. (4) two callers: a blocking `fetchRecent` parked on the same room is woken by `standDown()`'s waiter drain, not by this delivery, so suppressing the delivery cannot strand it.

summary: `existingRoom` — the read-only room resolver whose whole reason for existing is that "a read never provisions" — starts with `const cached = this.rooms.get(key); if (cached !== undefined) return cached;`. That map is shared with `ensureRoom`, which stores an in-flight `resolveOrCreateRoom` promise. So a `fetchRecent` concurrent with a first `post` on the same topic awaits the WRITE path's `POST /createRoom` and rejects with its error, instead of answering the empty page the README promises for a topic whose room does not exist. Synapse's ~2-room-burst-then-1-per-45s creation limit makes this the ordinary case, not an exotic one, and `buildBridge` awaits `catchUpAll`, so it fails startup.
failure: aliasExists=false, createRoom answering 429 M_LIMIT_EXCEEDED (as Synapse does). Issue `post(t, …)` and `fetchRecent({topic: t, limit: 10})` concurrently. Expected: post rejects, read returns `{messages: [], nextCursor: '@parley-stream:'}`. Actual (reproduced): the read rejects with `HttpStatusError: Matrix POST /_matrix/client/v3/createRoom → 429: still rate limited`.
remediation: In `existingRoom`, do not adopt the cached promise's rejection: `const cached = this.rooms.get(key); if (cached !== undefined) { const viaWrite = await cached.then((id) => id, () => undefined); if (viaWrite !== undefined) return viaWrite; }` and fall through to this method's own `lookupAlias` + generation-gated `adoptRoom`. A read then answers for itself when the write path's create failed, and still surfaces a refusal it reaches on its own.
testUpgrade: CLASS: a documented read-only path that can fail with a write path's error because the two share a memoization cell. Add a parameterized case in `provisioning.fake.test.ts` — a table over {which write path is in flight: post | subscribe} × {how it fails: createRoom 429, createRoom 400+unresolved alias, join 403, adoptRoom trust refusal} — that issues a concurrent `fetchRecent` and asserts the read either resolves to an empty page or rejects for a reason IT reached (assert on the error naming `/directory` or the trust bar, never `createRoom`). Existing coverage is too narrow because every provisioning row drives one seam call at a time, so the cache is never observed cross-path.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `ensureRoom`'s existing rejection handling — `.catch((err) => { this.rooms.delete(key); throw err; })` — which already removes the poisoned entry, so the read's fall-through resolve is not racing a permanently-bad cell. Also relies on `existingRoom`'s own `if (roomId === undefined || this.isStale(generation)) return undefined;` after `lookupAlias`, which is what turns the fall-through into the empty page.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: A `fetchRecent` that today rejects with `POST /createRoom → 429` now returns `{ messages: [], nextCursor: '@parley-stream:' }` (or the real page, if a peer created the room in between).
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found — I applied exactly this edit and ran the offline suite: 20 files / 1104 tests passed, including `provisioning.fake.test.ts`'s 'every seam call issues exactly the state changes it is declared to' and 'only a write provisions, and never into a world-joinable room', which are the two that pin read-path side effects. My repro flipped to `read-ok: 0`.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Fixes the leak. What it does NOT fix, and I want to be explicit: the read still BLOCKS for as long as the write path's create+retry takes before it gives up on the cached promise, because it awaits it. A caller with `blockMs: 0` therefore still pays the write path's 429 backoff in latency. Bounding that would need the cache to expose a settled-or-not view rather than a bare promise.
remediationCheck.interleavings: (1) read arrives before the write's promise settles → awaits it; on resolve it returns the id (unchanged), on reject it falls through and resolves independently. (2) read arrives after `ensureRoom`'s catch already deleted the key → cache miss, unchanged path. (3) two concurrent reads both fall through → both issue a `/directory` lookup and both may `adoptRoom` the same room; `POST /join` is idempotent and `this.rooms.set` is last-writer-wins with the same value, so the double work is wasteful but not incorrect. (4) a disconnect landing in the fall-through is caught by the existing generation gates on both sides of the join.

summary: `connect()` runs `access_token` through `adoptedString` — whose own doc says it exists so "a homeserver, a proxy or a captive portal answering the right status with the wrong body" cannot leave the plugin holding a bad value — and then adopts `user_id` with a bare `typeof … === 'string' ? … : undefined`. But `userId` is the sole self-entry in `trustedCreators`, so a 200 login without it silently collapses the room-adoption trust set to `invite` alone, and every alias that already resolves is refused. The refusal message then blames a hostile alias claim ("any account can claim it before this bridge does") for what is actually the plugin not knowing its own MXID.
failure: A homeserver (or proxy) answering `POST /v3/login` 200 with `{access_token: '…'}` and no `user_id`. Reproduced: `connect()` resolves, then the very first `post(asTopic('brick'), …)` rejects with `[parley-matrix] refusing the existing room #parley_brick:fake (!room0:fake): it was created by @parley:fake, which is neither parley nor any MXID in backend_config.invite` — for a room this account created.
remediation: `this.userId = adoptedString(json?.user_id, 'user_id', call);` alongside the token, so a login that mints no identity fails the `connect()` naming the call and the homeserver, rather than degrading a trust decision three calls later.
testUpgrade: CLASS: a value the plugin ADOPTS from a 200 and then treats as an invariant. `adopted-response.fake.test.ts` already has the right shape — a table of {field, malformed value} × {absent, '', non-string} — but its rows cover only `access_token` and `event_id`; `user_id` is present in every fixture body it builds. Drive that table from the set of fields `connect`/`post` read out of a 200 rather than a hand-list, and add an assertion arm for each that names the invariant the field anchors (token → no anonymous request; user_id → a room this session created is still adopted after a reconnect), so a new adopted field is a failing row the day it is added.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `adoptedString(raw, field, call)` in wire.ts: `if (typeof raw === 'string' && raw !== '') return raw; throw …` — the empty-string arm matters, since `''` would otherwise produce a `trustedCreators` entry that matches nothing.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: A `connect()` against a homeserver whose 200 login body omits or empties `user_id`. The Matrix C-S spec makes `user_id` required in a `POST /login` 200, so no conforming homeserver is newly rejected; a proxy or captive portal is.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: I did not run the suite with this edit in isolation (I ran it bundled with the server_name cross-check below, which broke 4 rows for its own reason). By inspection every fixture that reaches `connect()` supplies `user_id`: fake-synapse.ts's default login body, `adopted-response.fake.test.ts:145` and `:153`, `config-validation.test.ts:105`, `creds-warning.test.ts:14`. I would expect zero breakage, but I have not watched it — treat as untested.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Fixes the diagnosability half. It does NOT change the security posture: today's behaviour already fails closed (rooms are refused, not adopted), so nothing is being let through that this closes. The value is that an operator gets the true cause at connect() instead of a message accusing a third party.

summary: `validateConfig` checks `shared_room` against `LEGAL_LOCALPART` and the 255-byte alias bound precisely because "it is used verbatim" in the alias — and then checks `server_name`, the other verbatim half of that same alias, for nothing but non-empty-string. Worse, `connect()` already learns the homeserver's real domain from the login `user_id` and never compares it. A `server_name` that is misspelled, has a stray space, or simply names a different domain than the homeserver stamps produces `#parley_<topic>:<wrong>` for every topic: `createRoom` 400s and every read returns the empty page an unwritten topic returns, so the deployment silently never works. The package's own test helper `live-gate.ts:79` throws on exactly this mismatch, calling it "an unexplained skip or an empty room rather than the mis-set variable it is" — the fixture defends against it and the plugin does not.
failure: `backend_config: { server_name: 'has space' }` (or `'#hash'`, `'ok/slash'`, a NUL byte, an emoji, or simply `matrix.example.com` where the homeserver stamps `example.com`). Reproduced: `connect()` resolves with no error and `post()` puts `#parley_t:has space` on the wire as the directory lookup. Against a real Synapse that 404s forever and `createRoom` 400s.
remediation: Two parts, separable. (a) In `validateConfig`, hold `server_name` to the same bar `shared_room` gets: reject one that makes `aliasOf('x', server_name)` fail the alias grammar or the byte bound. (b) In `connect()`, after adopting `user_id`, compare the substring after its first `:` with `this.serverName` and throw naming both — the homeserver has just told you its own domain, and a room alias can only be created on it.
testUpgrade: CLASS: an operator-supplied component of a backend identifier that reaches the wire unchecked. `room-isolation.fake.test.ts`'s 'an alias reaches the wire legal however its localpart was chosen' already states the right invariant — 'the legality of a name this plugin addresses a room by does not depend on WHO chose it' — but drives it only over `shared_room`; `config-validation.test.ts`'s sweep varies `server_name` over three LEGAL values only. Re-parameterize both over the CROSS product {which alias component: derived localpart, shared_room, server_name} × HOSTILE_LOCALPARTS × length-boundary values, asserting one rule: loaded ⇔ every alias that reached `fake.directoryLookups`/`createRoomBodies` satisfies `aliasIsLegal`. Note `ALIAS_LEGAL`'s server half is currently `[^:]+`, which accepts spaces, `#`, `/` and NUL — that predicate has to be tightened first or the widened table passes vacuously.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `aliasOf(localpart, serverName)` and `MAX_ALIAS_BYTES` from alias.ts, already imported by config.ts for the `shared_room` branch; and `LEGAL_LOCALPART` only for part (a)'s localpart half — the server half needs its own pattern, since a legal `server_name` may carry a port (`host:8448`) that `LEGAL_LOCALPART` would reject.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: Part (a): a `server_name` carrying whitespace, `#`, `/`, NUL or an astral character, or one long enough to blow the 255-byte alias budget. Part (b): any config whose `server_name` differs from the domain the homeserver stamps on the logged-in MXID.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: I applied part (b) and ran the offline suite: 4 rows failed — `config-validation.test.ts` 'server_name = "parley.local": accepted', 'server_name omitted entirely: accepted', 'a shared_room loads exactly when the alias it builds is one Matrix can carry', and `room-isolation.fake.test.ts` 'a server_name leaving no room for a distinct localpart fails naming the plugin and the topic'. All four fail for the same fixture reason: `FakeSynapse` hard-codes `user_id: '@parley:fake'` regardless of the configured `server_name`, which no real homeserver does. Fixing the fake to stamp the configured domain is a prerequisite, and is itself a fake-fidelity improvement. I did not separately run part (a); by inspection no test supplies a hostile `server_name`, so I expect it clean, but that is untested.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Part (b) fixes the real-world case (a domain typo, or pointing at the wrong homeserver) and subsumes most of part (a) in practice, since a homeserver never stamps a domain with a space in it. Part (a) alone would still let a `server_name` that is grammatically fine but names the wrong server through — which is the failure an operator actually hits.

summary: `deliver` wakes only the waiters whose `waiter.topic === topic`. Deleting that condition — waking every waiter parked on the room — leaves all 20 offline files / 1104 tests green, and the live conformance suite too. Of 18 mutations I applied across this package, this was the only survivor. So the filter is either load-bearing and ungraded, or it is speculative: with `blockingFetch`'s spurious-wake re-arm loop, over-waking degrades a shared_room deployment into one `/messages` re-query per foreign-topic message rather than breaking anything, and nothing measures that.
failure: Mutation `for (const waiter of [...set]) waiter.wake();` (dropping `if (waiter.topic === topic)`) in src/index.ts:295 → `npx vitest run packages/bridge-matrix --exclude conformance --exclude live-per-topic` → 20 files passed, 1104 tests passed. The behaviour it is supposed to prevent (topic A's traffic amplifying topic B's parked long-poll into a re-query per message) is observed by no assertion.
remediation: Grade the cost, or delete the filter. Preferred: keep it and add the assertion — in shared_room mode, park a `fetchRecent({topic: B, blockMs})` and drive N messages on topic A through a `subscribe(A)` loop, then assert the number of `/messages` requests attributable to B's wait stays O(1) rather than O(N). `FakeSynapse.messagesRequests` already records exactly what is needed.
testUpgrade: CLASS: a filter whose only effect is on request volume, in a package where every other guard is graded on an outcome. `wake-source.fake.test.ts` proves waiters ARE woken (its whole point) but never that an unrelated topic's traffic does not wake them, so the mutation is invisible to it. Add a parameterized cost table to that file — rows over {same room + different topic, same room + same topic, different room} × {N foreign messages: 1, 20} — asserting `fake.messagesRequests.filter(u => u.searchParams.get('dir') === 'f').length` against a bound. Written that way it also covers the next wake-source added, not just this one.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `FakeSynapse.messagesRequests` (every `/messages` URL in order) and the `blockingFetch` re-arm loop's `for (const afterPark of [false, true])`, which is what issues a re-query per wake — the thing being counted.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: n/a — this is a test change, not a code change; the shipped behaviour is unaltered.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: n/a
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none — adding an assertion to a passing file. The risk is the opposite one: the bound has to be chosen against an observed count, or the new row is itself vacuous. I did not write the test, so the specific bound is untested.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Nothing is broken today; this closes a coverage hole. If the filter were instead deleted as speculative, the deployment cost above becomes real and nothing would notice — which is precisely why the measurement, not the deletion, is the right move.

summary: `MatrixPlugin extends MatrixParking extends MatrixTimeline extends MatrixSession` is a four-level chain in which each of the three abstract classes has exactly one implementation — it exists to spread one ~900-line class across four files, not for polymorphism. The cost is not aesthetic: fourteen `protected` mutable fields are in scope in every layer, so the generation/credential lifecycle has no single owner. That is the direct mechanism of the first finding here — `MatrixTimeline.backfill` re-derives `const generation = this.generation` while its siblings `fetchSince`, `drainForward` and `recentWindow` all take `generation` as a parameter, and nothing in the type system or the review surface makes the inconsistency visible.
failure: Not a runtime failure on its own. The observable consequence: `backfill(roomId, topic, prevBatch, stopAfter, skip)` is the only timeline method that does not receive the caller's generation, so after `connect()` with no preceding `disconnect()` a stale subscribe loop's backfill pages up to 50 authenticated `/messages` requests under the NEW generation's token before anything stops it.
remediation: Two cheap steps that do not require unwinding the hierarchy. (1) Make `generation` an explicit parameter on every protected method that outlives a round-trip — `backfill` is the one outlier — so the omission is a compile error rather than a silent `this.` read. (2) Longer term, replace the chain with composition: a `MatrixSession` value object (baseUrl/token/generation/http) held by the plugin and passed to free functions in `timeline.ts`/`park.ts`, which makes the mutable surface each function actually touches visible in its signature.
testUpgrade: CLASS: an inherited-state read where the caller's captured generation was intended. Add a source-level lint next to `comment-hygiene.test.ts` — which already globs `src/**` at any depth, so it survives a file move — asserting that no method whose body contains `await this.http(` also contains `this.generation` outside of a parameter default; the one legitimate capture site is `http()` itself. Written as a glob over `src/**` rather than a named file, per CLAUDE.md's rule that an architectural assertion must not cement the layout it observes.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: Step (1) relies on `backfill`'s existing loop guard `page < MAX_BACKFILL_PAGES && !this.isStale(generation)` — with a threaded generation this becomes false at page 0 for a stale loop, which is the desired narrowing.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: A stale subscribe loop's `limited`-burst recovery no longer runs at all. Those events remain reachable via `fetchRecent`, and the pre-existing `catch { /* backfill is best-effort */ }` already treats a failed backfill that way.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none for step (1) — I applied it (bundled with the first finding's `break`) and the offline suite passed 1104/1104. Step (2) is a refactor I did not attempt; I cannot say what it would break and am not claiming otherwise.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Step (1) closes the concrete generation leak. It does not address the underlying shared-mutable-state coupling, so the next method added to any layer can reintroduce the same class — which is what the proposed lint, not the refactor, is meant to hold.

summary: Two claims in this README do not match the code. (1) Both the README ("`@parley-stream:<pagination-token>`") and DESIGN.md §6 ("the second form `@parley-stream:<pagination token>`") describe the stream cursor as always carrying a token, and the README adds "These two are the only cursor forms the plugin emits" — but `emptyWindowCursor(undefined, undefined, false)` mints a bare, token-less `@parley-stream:`, which is what a since-less read of a topic with no room returns and what then lands in `read-state.json`. `shipped-artifacts.test.ts`'s 'every cursor form the plugin emits is documented' cannot catch it, because `cursor-shapes.ts` gives that shape the marker `'@parley-stream:'` — the prefix, which both docs contain either way. (2) The CLI paragraph says the default config file "names a different deployment's another homeserver, access token, handle and topic allowlist" — this backend's `backend_config` has no access token; it logs in with `user`/`password`. (The garbled "a different deployment's another X" is repo-wide boilerplate present in seven package READMEs; the wrong credential noun is matrix's own.)
failure: `await plugin.fetchRecent({ topic: asTopic('never-used') })` on a topic whose room does not exist returns `nextCursor === '@parley-stream:'`. An operator reading `read-state.json`, or an author of core-side tooling, looks that value up in the README or DESIGN §6 and finds a form described as carrying a pagination token — with no statement of what the empty one means (cursor.ts says it names "the first visible event in the room", i.e. replay the whole room). Meanwhile the README asserts these are the only forms emitted.
remediation: State the token-less form and its meaning in the README's cursor row and in DESIGN §6's Matrix bullet — 'a bare `@parley-stream:` names the room's first visible event and is minted only by a read of a topic whose room does not exist yet'. Fix 'access token' to 'user/password login' in the CLI paragraph.
testUpgrade: CLASS: a doc-coverage test whose key is coarser than the set it claims to cover. Give `cursor-shapes.ts` one entry per distinguishable form rather than per prefix — split 'stream token' into 'stream token (positioned)' with marker `@parley-stream:<` and 'stream token (room start)' with a marker naming the empty form — and add a `mint` field per shape holding a seam call that actually produces it, so `shipped-artifacts.test.ts` can assert every SHAPES entry is both reachable from the public surface and present in both docs. That makes the next form a failing row the day it is added rather than the day it confuses somebody.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `cursor.ts`'s `emptyWindowCursor`: `if (readAt !== undefined) return asCursor(PREFIX + readAt); if (sinceCursor !== undefined) return sinceCursor; if (stale) throw …; return asCursor(STREAM_CURSOR_PREFIX);` — the last line is the token-less mint, reachable only when a read observed no page and was given no `since` and is not stale.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none — documentation only.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none for the prose edits. Splitting `SHAPES` would fail `shipped-artifacts.test.ts`'s 'grades at least the two forms this plugin mints', which asserts `expect(documented).toHaveLength(2)`; that count has to move to three in the same change, and I did not run it.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Fixes the doc gap. It does not change behaviour: a bare `@parley-stream:` really does replay from the room's first visible event, which for a topic that later accumulates history means a since-less first read costs a full forward walk on the next catch-up. Whether that is the right behaviour is a separate question this remediation deliberately does not touch.

summary: `fetchRecent` takes its FIRST `readWindow` outside the armed-waiter window. `blockingMam` arms a waiter before each of its own re-reads, but the read at index.ts:197 that decides whether to block at all runs with no waiter registered, so a live groupchat message reflected during that query's round trip fires `fireWaiters` into an empty set. If the archive commit then lags past the next query's snapshot, `lagPoll` is still 0, the loop parks for the entire remaining budget, and the message is withheld until `block_ms` (up to core's `catchup.block_max_ms`, default 60 s) expires. Core's `fetchRecentBlocking` cannot rescue it — it is awaiting the plugin call that is parked.
failure: fetchRecent({topic, since: <tail>, blockMs: 3000}) with a 200 ms MAM round trip, a live reflection at t=50 ms (inside the first, unarmed query) and its archive commit at t=260 ms (inside the second query's in-flight window) returns `{messages: []}` after the full 3000 ms. Reproduced with a new test against FakeXmpp; with the fix applied the same input returns ['fresh'] in 653 ms.
remediation: Do not pre-read when blocking. In `fetchRecent`, compute `blockMs` first and call `blockingMam(topic, since, limit, blockMs)` for `blockMs > 0`, otherwise `readWindow` — dropping the `firstRead` parameter and seeding `let latest: ReadWindow = { items: [] }` in `blockingMam`, whose loop already arms the waiter before its first read. (Equivalent alternative: arm a waiter in `fetchRecent` before the pre-read and hand it to `blockingMam` as round one's waiter.)
testUpgrade: long-poll-wake.test.ts's `Stage` table is the right shape but its rows are defined by QUERY ORDINAL, so it cannot express "during the first query" once the first query moves. Re-express the table as the cross product of (which round trip the live copy lands in: the first, a later one) x (archival lag: 0, 50, 400, 1000 ms) x (MAM round-trip latency: 0, 200 ms), with the trigger keyed on the plugin's observable state (a waiter registered for the room) rather than on a query counter, and bound every cell's latency by `2*lag + overhead` and never by `blockMs`. That widened generator also covers the arm-after-the-recheck variants the current rows do cover.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `blockingMam`'s loop head — `if (this.stopped || Date.now() >= deadline) return latest;` then `const waiter = this.armWaiter(room);` then `latest = await this.readWindow(...)`. I depend on the branch where, with blockMs > 0, the deadline check is false on entry so at least one armed read always happens; and on `fetchRecent`'s existing `messages.at(-1)?.cursor ?? (window.tail === undefined ? (args.since ?? asCursor('')) : ...)` still producing the caller's own cursor for a `{items: [], tail: undefined}` window.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: none — the same arguments are accepted; only the read's ordering relative to the waiter changes.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none. One behaviour change short of rejection: a plugin already `stopped` when a blocking fetch starts now returns an empty page carrying the caller's cursor instead of throwing from the pre-read, which is the arm long-poll-wake.test.ts's disconnect table already permits and asserts.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: Applied the fix and ran the package suite: exactly one failure — `long-poll-wake.test.ts > XMPP long-poll wakeup > returns promptly when a message lands 'in-flight-of-the-recheck'`. It breaks for a fixture reason, not a behavioural one: its hook delivers only on the SECOND MAM query (`if (++queries > 1)`), and after the fix there is only one query before the park, so the message is never delivered at all. That row must be re-keyed to the state it means to reach (see testUpgrade). The other 1836 tests pass.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Nothing is hidden. If a wake were still lost on some other path, the caller would still wait out the whole budget — the fix closes only the pre-read window, and the parked round's own arm-before-read ordering is what covers the rest.
remediationCheck.interleavings: (a) live message lands during the first armed read, archive commits later: the fire hits a registered waiter, park returns 'message', lagPoll = 50 ms and doubles. (b) live message lands after park is armed: same waiter, same path. (c) two concurrent fetchRecent callers on the same room: `armWaiter` adds a distinct `fire` to the room's Set and each removes only its own, deleting the map key only when the Set empties, so one caller's cancel cannot deafen the other — unchanged by this fix. (d) disconnect landing between the deadline check and the first read: the read throws, the `catch` sees `stopped` and returns `latest`, and `finally` cancels the waiter.

summary: `switchNick` re-enters every joined room with `await Promise.allSettled(rooms.map((r) => this.ensureJoinedRoom(r)))` and discards every rejection. Every other path that re-drives a join reports — `redriveJoin` logs, `onOccupancyLost` logs and arms the backoff ladder — but the nick-adoption path does not, and it cannot arm the ladder either (`onOccupancyLost` early-returns on `!this.joined.has(room)`, and `ensureJoinedRoom`'s catch has already dropped the cache). A subscribed topic whose re-join bounces during the first `post`'s nick adoption loses live push permanently, with nothing on stderr and a successful `post` returned to the caller.
failure: connect(); subscribe(A); subscribe(B); then post(A, handle 'alice', 'hello') with the MUC answering the next two join presences `forbidden`. Result: post resolves successfully, `joined` no longer holds room-b, a subsequent `fake.deliver(room-b, ...)` reaches no handler, and `console.error` is called ZERO times about room-b. Reproduced against FakeXmpp.
remediation: Replace the `allSettled` with a per-room `catch` that reports on stderr in the same shape `redriveJoin` uses, naming the room, the condition and the consequence ("live push for this topic stays dead until a post or fetch_recent re-enters the room"). Restoring push, rather than only reporting, needs a scheduling decision — the honest options are to route the failure through the existing backoff ladder (which requires `onOccupancyLost` to accept a room already evicted from `joined`) or to leave recovery to the next seam call as the message says.
testUpgrade: diagnostics.test.ts already has one case ("reports a re-join that fails after a reconnect instead of swallowing it") — the class is "a join re-driven for ANY reason must report its failure", and the suite pins only one reason. Parameterize it over every re-drive trigger: reconnect (`online` #2), remote occupancy loss (the ladder timer), a post bounced with a not-an-occupant condition, and nick adoption via the first `post` — each asserting a stderr line that names the room, and asserting the subscribed topic's push state afterwards so a test cannot pass on the log alone.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `ensureJoinedRoom`'s rejection path — `p.catch(() => { if (this.joined.get(room) === p) this.forgetRoom(room); })` — which already drops the cache, so the added `catch` only observes; and `wire.asError(err).message`, which for a `JoinError` yields "MUC join error (forbidden) for <room>".
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none — `Promise.all` over handlers that all resolve behaves exactly as `allSettled` did; `switchNick` still never rejects, so `adoptIdentityNick`'s awaited promise still cannot reject a caller's `post`.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: Applied the fix and ran the package suite: 1837/1837 pass (the single failure in that run was finding 1's fixture coupling, from the other fix applied simultaneously). I specifically checked diagnostics.test.ts's `expect(errors).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1)` case — it never adopts a nick, so it is untouched — and the other nine files that spy on console.error assert `toContain`/`toMatch` on specific lines rather than a total count.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Reporting does NOT restore live push: the subscribed room stays outside its room until an unrelated later post or fetchRecent re-enters it. It converts a silent permanent outage into a loud one. If the underlying inability to re-join persists, the topic is still dead.
remediationCheck.interleavings: (a) two concurrent first-posts under different handles: the second sees `nickAdoption` already set and awaits the same promise, so the new catch runs once per room, not twice. (b) a `subscribe` racing the switch: it awaits its own pre-switch join promise, which still resolves; the room it is subscribed to is separately re-driven by the loop, and a failure there is now reported. (c) disconnect during the switch: `ensureJoinedRoom` rejects from `require()`, the catch logs a line during teardown — noisier than before, but not a hang.

summary: The shared conformance clause is "post either round-trips content exactly or refuses it". This backend does neither for a carriage return: `assertXmlSafe` deliberately admits U+000D, the serializer emits it raw, and XML 1.0 §2.11 line-end normalization turns it into LF before any reader sees it — a silent alteration of caller content. Rather than the backend conforming, the shared suite was narrowed around it: packages/conformance/src/cases/post.ts:9-14 carries a comment naming `bridge-xmpp` and omitting the CR row "because adding it first only reddens the backend". A shared contract that names one plugin as its reason for a hole is the seam smell the prime directive is about, and it means no CI-runnable test grades this behaviour at all (content-fidelity.test.ts pins it, but `describe.skipIf(!up)` skips without a live server).
failure: post(topic, handle, 'a\rb') resolves successfully; fetchRecent(topic) returns content 'a\nb'. The caller is told the write succeeded and is never told the bytes changed.
remediation: Refuse it up front, which is the arm the clause already permits: extend the pre-send check in `post` to reject U+000D in content with an error naming the codepoint and the reason (the plugin already has `codepointLabel` and the `attributeNormalizedCodepoint` precedent for exactly this class of in-transit rewrite). Then add the CR row to the shared suite and delete the backend-naming comment. The real cost, which must be weighed: a caller pasting Windows-line-ending text starts getting errors where it previously got usable LF text, so the alternative — keep normalizing but make the seam say so — is a legitimate adjudication, and if it is taken the fix belongs in the shared clause, not in a comment about one plugin.
testUpgrade: Parameterize the conformance post-fidelity table over a codepoint-class axis rather than a hand-picked list: for each of {CR, CRLF, LF, TAB, NEL U+0085, LS U+2028, astral pair, combining sequence, leading/trailing spaces}, assert the same binary — refused with a message naming the codepoint, or read back byte-identical. That row set catches the next transport whose serializer rewrites a different codepoint class, which a fixed five-row list cannot.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `wire.assertXmlSafe(content, 'post content')` at index.ts:152, and `xmlIllegalCodepoint`'s explicit `if (cp === 0x9 || cp === 0xa || cp === 0xd) continue;` — the branch that admits CR today and would have to be split so that CR is refused for content while remaining legal XML for everything else.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: post content containing U+000D — including every CRLF pair, i.e. ordinary text copied from a Windows editor, which today succeeds and stores LF.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: content-fidelity.test.ts rows 'a bare CR', 'a CRLF pair' and 'CR and CRLF mixed', plus 'the live path sees the same bytes as catch-up' — all four assert the CURRENT normalize-to-LF behaviour and all four would have to be rewritten to assert refusal. They are `skipIf(!up)`, so they are green-by-skip without a server; I did not run them against a live Prosody. xml-hostile-content.test.ts's payload `{ name: 'tab, newline and carriage return', legal: true }` would also flip for the post-content field.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If applied while the underlying constraint remains, nothing about XML is fixed — CR still cannot traverse an XMPP body. The change converts a silent mutation into a visible refusal, and moves the cost onto callers that send CRLF.

summary: README lines 30-37 claim `fetchRecent` "holds up to block_ms for a new message before returning" and that block_ms "changes only WHEN the call returns". `fetchRecent` reads `args.blockMs` only after the `roomExists` gate: for a topic whose MUC room has not been created yet — the exact case an agent long-polls a fresh topic — it returns at line 193 immediately, having never looked at `blockMs`. This is the same class the file's own test header calls out ("an argument honoured on only ONE arm of the call it belongs to") in its since/since-less form; the room-existence arm was not included. Core's `fetchRecentBlocking` degrades it to a poll at `block_poll_interval_ms` rather than a hang, so the cost is a disco#info probe per poll interval instead of one native wait — but the README sentence is not true of this arm.
failure: fetchRecent({topic: <never-posted-to>, blockMs: 60000}) returns `{messages: [], nextCursor: since ?? ''}` in one disco#info round trip instead of holding, and then does so again on every core poll for the whole 60 s.
remediation: Either honour the argument — re-probe existence inside the blocking loop (park the budget in slices and re-run `roomExists`, still never joining) — or state the exception in the README's block_ms paragraph: "a topic whose room does not exist yet returns at once; core's poll wrapper supplies the wait." Separately, gapFill must stop treating a short page as a closed gap: readWindow already computes `sawRecords`; it should also report whether it stopped because history ran out or because the anchor could not advance, and gapFill must keep `needsGapFillFrom` armed in the second case.

summary: `timedWait`'s post-registration `if (this.stopped) release();` carries a load-bearing risk comment ("Keep the `stopped` re-check after the registration, so that a teardown racing the arming cannot leave the wait parked with nothing left to release it") but no execution path can reach it in a stopped state: both callers — armWake's `if (conn.stopped || conn.generation !== generation)` early return, and interruptibleDelay's `if (this.stopped || ms <= 0) return` — test `stopped` in the SAME synchronous turn as the timedWait call, with no await between. The repo's own untrusted-payload.test.ts states the rule this breaks: "a defensive clause no fixture can reach is counted as coverage and grades nothing."
failure: Deleting the line leaves all 21 files / 1306 tests green. Do not leave a documented-as-load-bearing clause that nothing can execute.

Parameterizing over the primitives is what guards the class — a new primitive gets a row the day it is declared — rather than pinning this one line.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: close()'s ordering: `stopped = true` precedes `for (const abort of this.pendingAborts) abort(); this.pendingAborts.clear();`, which is what makes an arm-after-close leak; and armWake/interruptibleDelay's synchronous guards, which are what make it unreachable today.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: If the fail-fast option is taken, a future caller arming a wait on a closed connection now throws where it previously returned a wait that resolved immediately. That is a behaviour change for a path nothing currently takes.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found — I ran the full suite with the line deleted and all 1306 passed, which is the whole point of the finding.

remediationCheck.interleavings: The interleaving the comment names is: caller reads `stopped === false`; close() runs `stopped = true`, fires and clears pendingAborts; caller then registers into pendingAborts and parks. No current caller yields between its check and its registration, so no two callers can produce it. A fail-fast assertion is safe under both orderings because it only reads `stopped`.

summary: `close()` does `await Promise.race([Promise.allSettled(exits), delay(TEARDOWN_TIMEOUT_MS)])`. When the loops exit promptly — the normal case — the losing `delay(2000)` timer is neither cleared nor unref'd (net-util's `delay` is a bare `new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, ms))`), so it keeps Node's event loop alive for up to 2s after `disconnect()` has resolved. Invisible to the CLI, which calls `process.exit(0)`; visible to any embedder that imports ZulipPlugin and expects the process to end after disconnect.
failure: `await new ZulipPlugin().connect({site_url}); await plugin.disconnect();` in a plain script: disconnect resolves immediately but the process does not exit for a further ~2s (one pending macrotask). Same for every disconnect in a long-lived host, which accumulates a 2s timer per teardown.
remediation: Give the race a cancellable timeout — either an `unref()`ed timer, or a small helper that clears the timer in a `finally` after the race settles. The cleanest shared fix is in net-util: export a `delayCancellable(ms): { waited: Promise<void>; cancel(): void }` (or have `delay` accept `{ unref: true }`), since the same `Promise.race([work, delay(n)])` shape appears across the HTTP backends.
testUpgrade: A parameterized case over every plugin that exposes disconnect: after `connect(); disconnect()`, assert `process.getActiveResourcesInfo()` (or a timer count captured before connect) shows no residual timer. That guards the class — a teardown that leaves a timer, a socket or an interval behind — rather than this one call site, and it would also catch the same shape reintroduced elsewhere.

remediationCheck.newlyRejects: Nothing. An unref'd timer still fires if anything else keeps the loop alive, so the race's semantics are unchanged whenever the timeout is the arm that matters.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found — I checked operability.test.ts's 'disconnect completes in bounded time' rows and subscription-lifecycle.test.ts's teardown timing assertions; both measure when disconnect RESOLVES, which this does not change. Not verified by running.

summary: A blocking fetchRecent parked on its waiter is woken by connect()'s forgetTopics(), then resumes and re-queries using the NEW session's channel_map. The `this.stopped` guard on line 127 exists for exactly this and cannot fire, because connect() is synchronous end to end and has already set stopped back to false by the time the woken continuation runs. The gateway half of this axis is tabled exhaustively (gateway-budget.test.ts PARKED_DIALS x RETIREMENTS, whose comment names 'connect() leaves stopped false' as the trap); the seam-call half has no cell at all.
failure: connect({channel_map:{chat:A}}); post to A -> tail; subscribe; deliver 'B-secret-1','B-secret-2' into channel B; parked = fetchRecent({topic:'chat', since:tail, blockMs:3000}); 150ms later connect({channel_map:{chat:B}}). Reproduced: parked resolves with messages ['B-secret-1','B-secret-2'] labelled topic 'chat', and nextCursor = channel B's snowflake. Core persists B's cursor for topic 'chat'; because Discord snowflakes are globally time-ordered, that cursor sits ahead of channel A's history, so if the map is restored A's messages between `tail` and that cursor are never returned again. The plugin refuses the spatial form of this (session.ts:98, 'the same Discord message can never cross the seam under two topic labels') and permits the temporal form.

testUpgrade: Parameterize a 'a seam call in flight across a session boundary answers its OWN session or nothing' table, crossing ENTRY POINT (fetchRecent no-since, fetchRecent since, fetchRecent blocking-parked-on-waiter, a multi-page walk parked between pages via holdNextPage, post, subscribe, resolveIdentity) x RETIREMENT (disconnect(), connect() alone, disconnect()+connect()) x WHAT MOVED (channel_map re-pointed to a different populated channel, api_url re-pointed to a second fake, token changed). Each cell asserts the call returns only content from the channel its own session named, and that nextCursor is either the `since` it was given or a cursor from that channel. rest-contract.test.ts's 'two topics that fold to one channel' ENTRY_POINTS table is the right shape but only covers the spatial collision; gateway-budget.test.ts's RETIREMENTS axis is the right lifetime axis but only grades dials, sockets and IDENTIFYs.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: session.ts connect()'s existing synchronous prologue (`this.stopped = true; this.gateway.restart(...); this.forgetTopics();`) — the generation bump goes beside the epoch bump; and index.ts:127's existing `if (this.stopped || Date.now() >= deadline) return first;` branch, which already returns the pre-wait page as a legal empty answer.

remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: It fixes the waiter arm only. Left broken if applied alone: `pager()` re-resolves `this.channelId(topic)` on EVERY page, so a >100 walk that spans a connect() still switches channels between pages; and subscribe(), which does `this.subs.set(channelId, ...)` before awaiting ensureUp and the channel check, still wires (or silently loses) a subscription across a session swap.
remediationCheck.interleavings: Two orderings matter. (a) connect() during `await withDeadline(this.gateway.ensureUp(), blockMs)`: on resume isLive() is false because gateway.stop() cleared this.ws, so no waiter is armed and the guard is not reached — the call falls through to fetchWithin, which still uses the new map, so the pager capture is the arm that covers this one. (b) connect() during `await waiter.fired` or during the first fetchWithin: forgetTopics() calls wake() before waiters.clear(), the fire() resolves, and the continuation is a microtask that necessarily runs after connect() returns — so the generation read is always the post-connect value and the guard always fires. Two callers parked on the same channel share nothing mutable: each arm() allocates its own one-shot closure and each captures its own `generation` local.

summary: `runFetch` delegates the seam's exclusive-`since` contract entirely to `conversations.history {oldest}` and never checks the result against its own comparator. Every sibling contract in the same loop IS checked and throws (newest-first ordering, repeated page cursor, page ceiling, usable `ts`); this one is trusted. A server that ignores or mishandles `oldest` makes `nextCursor` move BACKWARDS and then stick, wedging the topic silently and permanently.
failure: Probe (fake patched to ignore `oldest`, plugin unmodified): channel of 10 messages, `fetchRecent({topic, since: '1788347561.000005', limit: 3})` repeated four times. Every call returns the same page [m0,m1,m2] and the same `nextCursor` '1788347561.000003' — BELOW the cursor it was handed. Core stores that, calls again with it, and gets the identical answer forever: catch-up never reaches m5..m9 and never errors.
remediation: In the per-entry loop in `runFetch`, alongside the existing `previousTs` ordering throw, add: `if (args.since !== undefined && compareTs(m.ts, args.since) <= 0) throw new SlackShapeError('conversations.history', `returned ${m.ts} at or below oldest ${args.since}; the window is not exclusive`);`. A throw rather than a filter keeps it consistent with the ordering guard: a walk that cannot trust the vendor's window refuses instead of publishing a cursor derived from it.
testUpgrade: CLASS: any request parameter whose effect the plugin's cursor arithmetic depends on but never verifies. Give `FakeSlack` a `setWindowHonesty('exclusive' | 'inclusive' | 'ignored')` axis parallel to the existing `setHistoryOrder`, and add a table row per mode crossed with the existing `SINCE_MODES`/`LIMITS` in catchup-window.test.ts: 'exclusive' drains as today, 'inclusive' and 'ignored' must REJECT naming `conversations.history`, and in no mode may `compareTs(nextCursor, since) < 0`. Existing coverage is too narrow because history-order.test.ts varies only the ORDER of a page the fake always filtered honestly, so no row can distinguish a checked window from an unchecked one.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `compareTs` from ./messages.js (already imported and used two lines above for the `previousTs` guard) and `SlackShapeError` from ./api.js (already imported and thrown for the ordering guard). It depends on the branch `args.since !== undefined`, the same condition that sets `body.oldest` at line 61.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: A `conversations.history` page containing any entry whose `ts` is <= the `since` the call sent — including the boundary entry itself, i.e. a server behaving inclusively. Today those entries are collected and can drive `nextCursor` below `since`.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none — I applied exactly this patch and ran `npx vitest run packages/bridge-slack`: 18 files, 1069 tests, all green. The fake filters `oldest` exclusively for every orderable entry, and every plugin-accepted `ts` (TS_RE) is a subset of the fake's `isOrderable` regex, so no fixture ever returns an at-or-below entry.

The sibling field two methods away gets this right (`body.reply_broadcast === 'true' || body.reply_broadcast === true`), so the omission is local, not a design choice.

summary: `requireUsableSocketUrl`'s downgrade refusal interpolates the configured `api_url` verbatim. `isHttpUrl` accepts a URL with HTTP-basic userinfo, so a `https://user:pass@proxy/api` endpoint has its password embedded in a `SlackShapeError` that propagates out of `subscribe` / a blocked `fetchRecent` into core, i.e. into the MCP tool result the model reads and into the operator's stderr. The package ships `plaintextRemoteOrigin` (which deliberately reports only `protocol//host`, dropping userinfo) and net-util ships `redactUrls` for exactly this hazard; the VENDOR url in the same message is reduced to an origin and the test table even asserts the Socket Mode ticket never appears — only the operator's own url is passed through raw.

Add a local `originOf = (u: string): string => { try { const { protocol, host } = new URL(u); return `${protocol}//${host}`; } catch { return '<unparseable api_url>'; } }` and interpolate `originOf(apiUrl)`. `URL.host` excludes userinfo, so the operator still gets the actionable half (which endpoint was configured) and the credential never leaves the process.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `new URL(...)` and its `protocol`/`host` getters. It does not reuse `plaintextRemoteOrigin` because that returns `undefined` for the secure api_url this branch is about — reading its return here would print `undefined`.

summary: `blockForMessage` arms a waiter, then `await this.runFetch(...)`. Every NORMAL exit clears it (`wake()` on data, the rung timer, `drainWaiters` on socket loss or `stop()`), but the REJECTING exit does not: if the ladder re-query throws — `NoSuchTopicError`, `SlackShapeError`, a 429 that exhausts the retry budget — the rejection propagates out of `fetchRecent` with the waiter still registered in `link.waiters` holding a live timer. The suite states this invariant explicitly ('a settled `fetchRecent({blockMs})` must leave none') but `withBlocking` only wraps calls that resolve, so no row can see it.
failure: Probe: channel exists, `fake.onHit('conversations.history', hit => { if (hit === 1) fake.failMethod('conversations.history','channel_not_found') })`, then `plugin.fetchRecent({topic, since: asCursor('0'), blockMs: 3000})`. The call rejects with NoSuchTopicError and `parkedWaiters(plugin)` returns 1 instead of 0 — a registered waiter with a live setTimeout, iterated by every later live event on that channel until its rung elapses (<=5s) or `disconnect()` drains it.
remediation: Wrap the re-query so the waiter is always released on the way out: `let requeried; try { requeried = await this.runFetch({ ...args, since: floor }); } catch (e) { wake(); throw e; }` — or hoist the whole loop body's post-arm section into a `try { ... } finally { if (!consumed) wake(); }`. `wake()` is idempotent (`if (done) return`), so calling it on the success path as well is harmless.
testUpgrade: CLASS: a registry entry whose cleanup is attached only to the success path. Add a REJECTING axis to `withBlocking` in blocking-fetch.test.ts — a table of ways a ladder re-query can fail (`channel_not_found`, `not_in_channel`, a shape error via `seedRaw` returning `messages: {}`, a 429 storm) — and assert `parkedWaiters(plugin) === 0` after the rejection, by capturing the call with `capture()` rather than awaiting it. The same axis retro-fits to any future per-call registry the link grows.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `armWaiter`'s returned `wake`, whose `done` flag (link.ts:157) makes a second call a no-op, and its `set.delete(waiter)` + `clearTimeout(timer)` cleanup path.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none; the rejection still propagates unchanged, it just no longer leaves state behind.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found. I looked at every `parkedWaiters` call site (harness.ts:92, blocking-fetch.test.ts:67 and :437) and both assert the count is 0; making the count reach 0 in one more case cannot fail them. No test asserts a non-zero waiter count anywhere in the package. Untested — I did not run the patched version.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: It restores the stated registry invariant. If left unfixed the leak is self-healing within one ladder rung (<=5s) and is also drained by `disconnect()`, so the standing cost is a handful of stale waiters and timers under a repeatedly-failing topic — real but bounded, which is why this is a suggestion rather than blocking.
remediationCheck.interleavings: The interleaving that matters is `disconnect()` landing between `armWaiter` and the `runFetch` rejection: `stop()` drains and clears the map first, so my `wake()` then finds no set for the channel and only clears its own timer and resolves — safe. Two callers on the new path each hold their own `wake` closure over their own `waiter`, and `Set.delete` of an absent member is a no-op, so neither can clear the other's registration.

summary: `Diagnostics.lastReportAt` is an unbounded Map whose key is composed from a caller-chosen topic string (`unresolved-topic:${t}` in chats.ts:42). Entries are never evicted and never cleared — the Diagnostics instance is a `readonly` field on TelegramPlugin, so it outlives `disconnect()`. This is exactly the class ObservedStore bounds with SERVED_ID_MEMORY, and store.ts:38 states the reason: core's allowlist admits `post_topics` regex patterns, so the topic space is model-chosen rather than operator-sized.
failure: Reproduced: 500 `fetchRecent` calls on topics `not-a-chat-0`..`not-a-chat-499` grew the map from 0 to 500 entries; after `disconnect()` it was still 500. Each unresolvable topic (up to MAX_MATCH_INPUT = 64 chars via a post_topics pattern) permanently costs ~100 bytes of heap, with no bound and no release path short of process exit.
remediation: Bound `lastReportAt` inside `Diagnostics.report`: after `set`, evict oldest-first while `size > N` (Map iterates insertion-order, the same idiom `rememberEvicted`/`rememberServed` already use), with N a named constant beside the 60s window. Alternatively drop the topic from the `kind` and key on a fixed `'unresolved-topic'` — but that trades away the per-class independence the JSDoc promises, so the LRU bound is the smaller change.
testUpgrade: Parameterize a case over every seam entry point that can build a `kind` from caller input (`post`, `fetchRecent`, `subscribe`) x an unresolvable-topic generator, driving >2N distinct topics and asserting the plugin's internal throttle state stays <= N and that it is empty (or bounded) after `disconnect()`. Generalize it as a lint over `src/**`: every `Map`/`Set` whose key is interpolated from a `Topic`/`Handle`/`BackendMsgId` must have an eviction site. `seam-driven-state.test.ts` already grades this class for the store's served marks but stops at the store, so it could not have caught it here; widen that file's METHODS table to also assert the diagnostics bound.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `Map` insertion-order iteration, already relied on by `ObservedStore.rememberEvicted` ("Hold the newest {@link EVICTED_ID_MEMORY} evicted ids, newest last (Set iterates in order)"). Nothing in Diagnostics.report is re-entrant.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: none — no input is accepted that is rejected today.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none. It changes only retention: after N distinct kinds, the oldest kind's last-report timestamp is forgotten, so that kind may print again sooner than 60s if it recurs.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found. I checked `poll-loop.test.ts` 'throttles a persistent failure to one diagnostic per minute' and 'throttles each failure kind independently' (both use 2-3 fixed kinds, far under any sane N) and `docs.test.ts` 'writes a diagnostic when a topic resolves to no chat' (asserts on the message text, not on the throttle state).
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: Nothing stays broken — the growth is the whole defect. It does not address the sibling `ChatResolver.byTopic`/`byName` memos, which are also unbounded per topic, though I confirmed by probe that those ARE dropped at `disconnect()` (`this.chats = undefined`), so their lifetime is one connection.

The same package explicitly defends this class one module over: `canonicalChatKey` in wire.ts:73 routes an upstream-chosen chat spelling through `sanitizeBody` with the comment "unbounded and unflattened it is an attacker-chosen string with forged line structure in it". A topic reaches the plugin through `post`/`fetch_recent`, which core admits by `post_topics` regex — i.e. a model-chosen string — so it is the same threat, unguarded.

Reproduced: `plugin.fetchRecent({ topic: asTopic('ctx-a\nparley-telegram: SECURITY: token is 123:abc\nx') })` writes to stderr:
`parley-telegram: topic 'ctx-a`

— a forged second line carrying the plugin's own `parley-telegram:` prefix. The identical unflattened string is also in the rejected Error's `.message`, which the MCP tool hands back as model context.

Anchor it on the invariant rather than on chats.ts: assert over the plugin's public surface, so a new diagnostic in any module inherits it. `docs.test.ts` 'writes a diagnostic when a topic resolves to no chat' is the existing case that is too narrow — it only asserts the topic IS present, never how.

I did not execute the suite with the fix applied.

summary: `parseIds` calls `JSON.parse` outside any try, so a `#served`/`#evicted` line whose payload is not valid JSON throws into `load()`'s generic `catch`, sets `dropped = true`, and re-mints the store identity — refusing every outstanding cursor. A payload that IS valid JSON but not an array is quietly tolerated (`return []`). The same conceptual damage to the same kind of line gets opposite verdicts depending only on JSON syntax, and neither of these lines carries a record or a sequence, so losing one cannot cause a sequence to be re-issued — the thing the re-mint exists to prevent. `parseIds`'s own JSDoc states the tolerant behaviour ("or none when it is garbled"), which the code does not implement.
failure: Reproduced against a store file that loaded whole: appending `#served [not json` (or `#evicted [oops`) yields `store.epoch()` !== the previous identity plus `... did not load whole — a damaged or torn line could not be loaded` on stderr; every `fetchRecent` since-cursor an agent holds then fails with "was issued by a different observed-message store", on a backend with no history endpoint to re-derive from. The same file with `#served {"a":1}` keeps its identity.
remediation: Give `parseIds` the try/catch its doc describes — `try { ids = JSON.parse(...) } catch { return [] }` — so a damaged bookkeeping line degrades to "this protection/dedup memory did not survive" (reported, not silent) rather than to a cursor-space reset. Keep the re-mint for a damaged RECORD line, a damaged `#epoch` and a damaged `#seq`, which really do bear on sequence identity.
testUpgrade: Extend `store.test.ts`'s IDENTITY_DAMAGE table into a two-dimensional one: {line kind: record, #epoch, #seq, #served, #evicted} x {damage: absent, truncated, non-JSON, wrong JSON type, wrong arity} with an explicit `remints: boolean` column per cell, so every bookkeeping-line kind has a stated verdict and a new `#`-prefixed line type cannot land without one. Today no cell of that table covers `#served` or `#evicted` at all.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `load()`'s per-line `try { ... } catch { dropped = true; }` (store.ts:149-167) — the fix depends on `parseIds` no longer reaching that catch, and on the surrounding `rememberServed`/`rememberEvicted` accepting an empty array (they iterate, so they do).
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: A store file carrying a syntactically-broken `#served`/`#evicted` line now loads under its ORIGINAL identity, so cursors issued before the damage are answered instead of refused.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: none.
remediationCheck.testsThatWouldFail: none found — I checked `store.test.ts` IDENTITY_DAMAGE (only `#epoch` rows), DAMAGED (record rows only), TORN_TAILS (its `#served ["1"]` row is a WELL-FORMED served mark, so it does not reach the JSON.parse failure path), and the SERVED_PERSISTENCE/SERVED_MARK tables (well-formed lines). I did not execute the suite with the fix applied.
remediationCheck.hidesOrFixes: If the fix is applied and the real problem were instead that a damaged `#evicted` line loses dedup memory, that loss becomes silent unless the fix also reports it — so the remediation should report the drop, not just swallow it. It does not change the verdict for a damaged `#seq` or `#epoch`, which stay loud, correctly.

summary: `CADENCE_CELLS` crosses `poll_timeout_s` in {1, 25, 50} with 4 misbehaviours, but `timeoutS` reaches only two places in `pollUpdates`: the `timeout=` query parameter and `budgetMs = timeoutS*1000 + max(2000, timeoutS*400)`. All four misbehaviour rows arrange for the fake to answer immediately (`ignoreLongPoll`, `ignoreOffset`, or a batch that acknowledges then goes empty under an ignored long poll), so the `timeout=` parameter is discarded upstream, and the measurement window is 1000 ms while the smallest `budgetMs` on the table is 3400 ms. The 25 and 50 rows therefore execute the same code as the 1 row and cannot fail independently — 8 of 12 cells, roughly 10 s of wall clock, discriminating nothing.
failure: Trace: for `pollTimeoutS` 25 vs 50 the only differing value is `budgetMs` (27 000 vs 52 000 ms), which is never reached inside the test's 1000 ms measurement; the assertions are `spent <= 8` and `spent > 0`, both governed solely by `MIN_IDLE_POLL_MS`. Any mutation that flips a 25-row also flips the 1-row, so the extra rows can never be the ones that go red.
remediation: Collapse the cadence table to one `poll_timeout_s` (the misbehaviour axis is what it grades), and if the `budgetMs` arithmetic needs a table, give it its own case whose measurement window straddles the budget — which is what 'does not abandon a healthy long poll at a shared per-call default' already does for the >30 s half.
