Matrix (config.ts:198), discord (creds.ts:23), nats (config.ts:260), redis (diagnostics.ts:108), slack (config.ts:247), xmpp (config.ts:81), zulip (index.ts:58), telegram (test/plaintext-api-url.test.ts) all classify and warn, five of them through the shared `plaintextRemoteOrigin`/`isLoopbackHost` in @sharptrick/parley-net-util. `grep -rn 'ssl|TLS|plaintext|SECURITY' packages/bridge-postgres/src/*.ts` returns exactly one hit — index.ts:94, which warns about the default CREDENTIAL VALUE, never about the TRANSPORT. bridge-postgres/README.md never says 'TLS' or 'sslmode'.
failure: backend_config: { url: 'postgres://parley:hunter2@db.example.com:5432/parley' }. `new Pool({ connectionString: this.url })` (index.ts:101) with no sslmode leaves node-postgres at ssl:false, so the password and every message body cross the network in cleartext. Nothing is printed. The identical shape on redis ('redis://user:pw@db.example.com') prints 'parley-redis: SECURITY: … carries a credential over plaintext redis:// to a non-loopback host'. The invariant is stated in five sibling packages and enforced in nine; postgres is the cell nobody filled.
remediation: Give bridge-postgres a `plaintextCredentialRisks(url)` built on net-util's `isLoopbackHost`: parse the DSN with pg-connection-string (already the parser config.ts:129 uses), and if it carries a user/password, resolves to a non-loopback host, and neither `sslmode` (>=require) nor `ssl` is set, write a stderr SECURITY line naming `backend_config.url`, the origin only (never the value), and `?sslmode=require`. Warning, not load error — the dev-compose loopback server must keep running.

Add a table there: for every such plugin whose declared config keys include a host-bearing key, connect() with (a) a loopback plaintext endpoint carrying a credential and (b) a non-loopback plaintext endpoint carrying the same credential, and assert stderr/console.warn is silent for (a) and names both the KEY and the ORIGIN — and never the secret — for (b). summary: `retention_days` is the same documented key in four backends with four incompatible acceptance contracts, and the SAME data-loss argument is spelled out in two of them and absent from the other two. I ran 11 values through sqlite's validateBackendConfig, redis's resolveConfig, postgres's validateBackendConfig and nats's validateRetentionMaxAgeNs. Divergent cells: null → redis ACCEPT ('forever'), other three reject. 1e-9 → sqlite reject, postgres reject, redis ACCEPT, nats ACCEPT. 0.0005 (43s) → sqlite reject, postgres reject, redis ACCEPT, nats ACCEPT. 1e6 → sqlite ACCEPT, redis/postgres/nats reject. Only 1/1440 and 7 agree.
failure: `backend_config: { retention_days: 0.0005 }`. On sqlite the load fails with 'a window this short deletes the whole history on the connect() prune, which is what 0 and negatives were already refused for'. On postgres it fails with the same sentence. On redis it is accepted, and the next `post` issues XADD with MINID at now-43s, silently trimming the entire stream. On nats it is accepted and the JetStream stream is created with max_age=43.2e9ns, locked in at creation. Symmetrically, `retention_days: 1000000` is refused by postgres ('puts the cutoff before any message this backend could have written, so pruning would silently never run') and accepted by sqlite, where pruning silently never runs. Each backend fixed its own cell; nothing propagated the class.
remediation: Put the shared numeric contract in one place both halves can read — a `normalizeRetentionDays(plugin, value, { min, max })` beside `assertKnownConfigKeys` in bridge-core (it is seam-shaped: core is handed a NAME and a number, never a meaning), with MIN_RETENTION_DAYS = 1/1440 and a max derived from the caller's representable ceiling. Each backend keeps its own extra bound (nats's int64 max_age, redis's epoch-days) as an additional clause, not as a replacement contract. Decide `null` once: either every backend reads it as 'forever' or none does.
testUpgrade: CLASS: a config key name shared by N backends whose acceptance contract differs. Add a table to packages/conformance/test/backend-config-keys.test.ts (which already derives the plugin set from the seam and the key set from each plugin's own refusal message, so neither half can go stale): for every key name declared by MORE THAN ONE plugin, run a fixed hostile-value corpus (null, 0, -1, 1e-9, 1e-12, 1/1440, 7, 1e6, 1e18, NaN, Infinity, '7', true, []) through every declaring plugin's connect() and assert the accept/reject verdict is IDENTICAL across them, or that the divergence is recorded in an explicit exception map with a reason. A floor asserting at least three keys are shared, so an empty table reds. No existing test covers this: sqlite, redis, postgres and nats each grade only their own validator, so all four are green on the matrix above.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: bridge-core/src/backend-config-keys.ts, which already exports `assertKnownConfigKeys(plugin, config, declared)` and is imported by every backend's config.ts — the same call site the new normalizer would sit beside; and sqlite's existing MIN_RETENTION_DAYS = 1/1440 with the reasoning already written at config.ts:61.
remediationCheck.newlyAccepts: `retention_days: null` on sqlite/postgres/nats, if null-as-forever is the contract chosen.
remediationCheck.newlyRejects: `retention_days: 1e-9` and `0.0005` on redis and nats; `retention_days: 1000000` on sqlite. Each of these is a value that today silently destroys or silently never prunes history.

summary: The repo's only guard against 'a file in one package reaching INTO another one by path' extracts paths with three regexes: a quoted literal, an UNINTERPOLATED template literal (`/`(\.\.?\/[^`\n$]*)`/` — the `$` exclusion is what closes it to interpolation), and a join/resolve form whose FIRST segment must be a quoted '..'. Every spelling that builds the path from a variable escapes it. This is not hypothetical: packages/bridge-xmpp/test/backend-config.test.ts:153 already writes `readFileSync(new URL(`../../../${path}`, import.meta.url))` and is invisible to the scan today; it happens to resolve inside its own package, so a one-token edit turns it into a cross-package coupling with the guard still green.

Same for a join/resolve whose segment list contains a non-literal after a leading '..'. Keep the comment-stripping as-is.

The existing planted-tree rows use only the literal and the segment forms, which is why they are green on all four escapes above.

summary: Three of four workflows declare least-privilege GITHUB_TOKEN scopes (pr-title: pull-requests:read; publish-manual: id-token:write + contents:read; release: contents:write + id-token:write). ci.yml declares none at either workflow or job level, so both its jobs inherit the repository default. It is also the workflow that runs the most untrusted code: `npm ci` (which executes dependency install scripts, e.g. better-sqlite3's native build), `./examples/dev-compose/dev-infra.sh up all`, and `npm run preflight:publish` (which shells `npm view`/`npm pack`). Nothing in the suite reads a workflow's permissions block: packages/conformance/test/repo-contract.test.ts parses `on:`, `jobs:` and `run:`/`name:` steps and grades gate-vs-publisher step supersets, but `grep -n permissions packages/conformance/test/*.ts` returns nothing.

The drift is invisible to every reviewer and to the suite: add a fifth workflow with no permissions block tomorrow and nothing reds. Contrast release.yml, which spells out both scopes and why.
remediation: Add `permissions: contents: read` at the top of ci.yml (both jobs need nothing more — checkout, npm, docker, and a read-only registry query).

Include the planted-workflow positive control the neighbouring cases already use, so a parser that stops matching reds instead of passing on an empty scan.

remediationCheck.reliesOn: `jobsOf`/`triggersOf`/`publishes` in packages/conformance/test/repo-contract.test.ts:492-535, and specifically the `publishes(workflow)` branch that already distinguishes a publisher from a gate — that is what the allow-map keys on.

summary: `appFor` sets `process.env.NODE_ENV` and then awaits twice inside that window (`await freePort()`, `await door.boot(port, fx)` — which for `createOidcRemoteApp` performs a real HTTP discovery round trip). It also caches by `door.name|env` with a check-then-boot that is not atomic. Both are safe ONLY because nothing in the repo uses `it.concurrent` (grepped: zero hits under packages/bridge-core). The invariant is undocumented and the harness is exported to the whole package.
failure: Make any consumer of this harness concurrent — e.g. `describe.concurrent` in auth/error-surface.test.ts, or two `appFor` calls under `Promise.all` — and two outcomes follow. (a) Two calls for the same key both pass the `booted.get(key) === undefined` check and both bind a port; `booted.set` keeps one, so `closeFrontDoors()` never closes the other and the vitest worker holds a listening socket past the run. (b) Overlapping calls for different envs interleave inside the NODE_ENV window, so a door boots under a neighbour's env — and NODE_ENV is precisely the axis this matrix exists to grade (BOOT_ENVS, front-doors.ts:70, feeding Express's stack-rendering branch), so the production row can silently be graded as development and pass. I did not reproduce this: doing so requires editing the consuming test, which would be manufacturing the trigger rather than finding it.
remediation: Memoize the promise, not the result — `booted.set(key, promise)` before the first await, as `fixturesUp()` already does with `fixtures ??=` — and construct each app under an explicit env rather than a global: pass the env into `door.boot` and have each factory set it on the Express instance (`app.set('env', env)`) instead of mutating `process.env` across awaits. Also make `closeFrontDoors` close every server even if one rejects (`Promise.allSettled`), and clear `fixtures` before awaiting it so a rejected `startFakeOidc` cannot rethrow out of `afterAll` and skip teardown.
